subtype: Always and never after one event [Actor]
passage: During the Puja holidays, the lane behind Bidisha's building turned into a badminton court every evening, the net strung between two lamp posts wrapped in fairy lights. On Saturday the captains chose sides, and Bidisha was called last. She played anyway, missed two easy shots, and her team lost by three points. That night she refused to come down for the pandal visit. "I'm not going. Nobody ever picks me. I never win anything, ever," she told Devika, her older cousin, pulling the blanket over her head. Devika sat on the edge of the bed. "Last week you won the drawing contest at the pandal," she said. Bidisha kept her face hidden. "That was different. That doesn't count."

qa.q: What happened when the captains chose sides on Saturday?
qa.a: Bidisha was called last, and later her team lost by three points.

qa.q: Why does "Nobody ever picks me" feel true to Bidisha that night?
qa.a: Bidisha is hurt and embarrassed after being called last and losing, and the fresh sting is so big that one evening feels like her whole life; even the drawing-contest win "doesn't count".

qa.q: What could help Bidisha test her "never" rule?
qa.a: Devika or a parent could help her list other times she was picked or did win, like the drawing contest, and remind her that one Saturday game is one game, not every game.

qa.q: How might Devika see Bidisha's refusal to go to the pandal?
qa.a: Devika can see one bad game spoiling the whole holiday, and may feel sad and a little puzzled that a real win is being waved away.

grounding: A child picked last in one game stretches it into a rule that she is never chosen and never wins.

passage:
Friday, first day back after winter break

Fog so thick this morning that the bus crawled. Should have stayed in bed.
At lunch I carried my tray to the table by the window where Sanya's group sits. Before I could put it down, one of them said the seat was "saved". All five seats. For the whole term, apparently.
So that's that. Nobody in this school wants me around. Nobody anywhere will, probably. I'll just eat in the library till I finish Class 12.
Rehana from chemistry waved at me to come sit with her and her friends. I pretended I didn't see. She was only being polite anyway. People decide about me in five seconds and the answer is always no.

Leela

qa.q: What was Leela told at the table by the window?
qa.a: That the seat was "saved", and in fact all five seats were saved for the whole term.

qa.q: Why does Leela feel so sure that nobody will ever want them around?
qa.a: The refusal at lunch left Leela hurt and humiliated, and that single sting feels like proof about everyone; expecting "no" feels safer than risking another rejection.

qa.q: What small step could Leela take to test this belief?
qa.a: Next time Rehana waves, Leela could go and sit there for one lunch and notice that one table's answer is not the whole school's.

qa.q: How might Rehana see it when Leela pretends not to notice the wave?
qa.a: Rehana may feel ignored and think Leela doesn't want to join, which is the opposite of what Leela actually fears.

grounding: One group refuses Leela a seat, and Leela treats that single refusal as proof that no one will ever accept them.

passage:
Two days before the statistics exam, Marek sat in the university library in Kraków and told Xin not to bother helping. "I always freeze. Every exam, my head just goes white."
Xin pushed a sheet of paper across the table. "Fine. Write down every exam since September. Mark the ones you froze in."
Marek wrote six. He had frozen in two: the first chemistry midterm and last month's statistics quiz. The other four had gone fine, including a long oral exam.
"What was different in those four?" Xin asked.
Marek frowned at the list. Before the good ones he had slept, and he had started with the question he knew best. Before the bad ones he had crammed all night and begun with the hardest problem.
"So not always," he said slowly. "Mostly when I skip sleep and start with the worst question."
He circled both and wrote underneath: sleep, easy question first.

qa.q: How many of the six exams did Marek freeze in?
qa.a: He had frozen in two: the first chemistry midterm and last month's statistics quiz.

qa.q: Why does "I always freeze" feel true to Marek before the exam?
qa.a: Marek is anxious, and the two bad exams are so vivid that they feel like every exam, while the four that went fine fade from view.

qa.q: Why was Xin's list a useful countermeasure?
qa.a: Writing down every exam turned a vague "always" into countable cases, and comparing good and bad ones showed concrete things to work on: sleep and starting with an easier question.

qa.q: How might Xin feel watching Marek circle the two things?
qa.a: Xin is likely relieved and encouraged to see Marek move from "don't bother" to a plan he can actually use. 🙂

grounding: A student who believes they always freeze counts the counter-examples and finds what was different, which loosens the rule and shows what to work on.

subtype: One bad boss means all workplaces [Actor]
passage:
My name is Parul, and last monsoon I quit my first job after fourteen months under a manager who read our chats aloud in meetings and mocked anyone who asked a question. By the time the rains stopped I had a rule: offices are all like that. Every single one.
So when Eshaan forwarded me an opening at his design studio during Diwali week, I didn't even open the link. "They'll be nice in the interview," I told him, "and then it starts." He said his team leaves at six and the lead brings sweets for everyone. I said that's exactly what they want you to see.
Looking back, I had met exactly one manager. I had turned him into every manager in the city, and I didn't send a single application for four months.

qa.q: What did Parul do with the link Eshaan forwarded during Diwali week?
qa.a: Parul didn't even open the link.

qa.q: Why did refusing the opening feel sensible to Parul at the time?
qa.a: After fourteen months of being mocked, Parul felt wary and hurt, and expecting every office to be the same felt like protection from being hurt again.

qa.q: What could help Parul get past the "all offices" rule?
qa.a: Parul could treat the old job as one example and gather more, for instance by asking Eshaan's team specific questions about meetings and feedback before deciding.

qa.q: How might Eshaan feel when the link goes unopened?
qa.a: Eshaan may feel frustrated or sad that an honest description of the team is brushed aside, since the point was to offer Parul a way back into work.

grounding: After one harsh first job, the narrator decides all workplaces are toxic and stops applying, though the conclusion goes far beyond one manager.

passage:
Class 9 science fair, last week of Ramzan: note for my file.
Afreen's water-filter model drew a crowd all morning. I counted at least nine visitors who praised it. The judges liked the layered sand, two parents asked for the design, and the principal called it "properly thought through". One judge said the written report was too short.
At the end of the day Asif, her project partner, was grinning. Afreen was not. When I asked how it went, she said, "The report was bad. The judge said so." I asked what else people had said. She could remember only that one comment. She was fasting and tired, which did not help.
Next step: tomorrow I will go through the judges' sheets with her, every line, and let her mark the praise in green and the one fix in red.

qa.q: What did one judge say about Afreen's project?
qa.a: That the written report was too short.

qa.q: Why might the one criticism feel like the whole verdict to Afreen?
qa.a: The comment hurt, and hurt grabs attention; tired from fasting, Afreen feels disappointed and ashamed about the report, so the nine pieces of praise fade out.

qa.q: Is the teacher's plan a good countermeasure, and why?
qa.a: Yes. Going through every line and colouring the praise and the fix differently puts the whole picture back in view without pretending the criticism was never made.

qa.q: How might Asif see the same day?
qa.a: Asif, grinning, seems to remember the crowd and the praise, so Asif may be puzzled that Afreen looks so low after a day that felt like a success.

grounding: A teacher's note shows a teenager who got plenty of praise and one criticism but can recall only the criticism.

subtype: Only the negatives in a review [Actor]
passage:
Before, Thursday, a week before Holi: Dhruv spent three evenings preparing a coding workshop for first-years and told his roommate Abhinav he would be happy if even half of them understood loops.
During, Saturday: Twenty-six feedback forms came back. Twenty-five said clear, fun, or "best session this term". One had a drawn frowning face and the words "too fast". Dhruv read that one four times and put it on top of the pile.
After, the Tuesday after Holi, colours still on the hostel stairs: Abhinav asked if he would run another session. "No. They hated it," Dhruv said. "You saw the form." Abhinav pulled the pile across the table and began reading them out, one by one. Dhruv listened to four, then cut in: "Okay, but that frowning one—"

qa.q: What was written on the one frowning form?
qa.a: "Too fast", next to a drawn frowning face.

qa.q: Why does "They hated it" feel true to Dhruv on Tuesday?
qa.a: Dhruv is hurt and disappointed by the one critical form; he read it four times and kept it on top, so it feels bigger than the twenty-five happy ones.

qa.q: What could Dhruv do with the forms to see them more fairly?
qa.a: Dhruv could sort and count them, treat "too fast" as one specific fix such as slowing down on loops, and keep the praise in view when deciding about another session.

qa.q: What is it like for Abhinav when Dhruv says "They hated it"?
qa.a: Abhinav seems puzzled and a bit frustrated, because the forms plainly show a successful session, so Abhinav starts reading them out loud.

grounding: A student fixes on one frowning comment among many good ones, so a successful workshop feels like a failure.

passage:
Wednesday night

Ramesh's half-year review today. Honestly one of the best I've written: he shipped the billing fix early, juniors go to him first, two clients ask for him by name. One line said his status updates could be shorter.
He walked out of the room looking like I'd fired him. At tea he said, "So I'm too slow with updates. Got it." Not a word about the rest.
I felt awful, like I'd written it badly. So I called him back in, put the page between us and read the whole thing aloud, every line, slowly. Then I asked, "What else does this page say?"
He was quiet for a long time. Then: "That... people rely on me?"
Tomorrow I'll send it again with the good parts first.

Usha

qa.q: Which line in the review did Ramesh fix on?
qa.a: The line saying his status updates could be shorter.

qa.q: What was Usha feeling when Ramesh walked out of the room?
qa.a: Usha felt awful and a little guilty, worried the review had been written badly, because a mostly glowing review had landed as criticism.

qa.q: Why did reading the whole page aloud help?
qa.a: It made Ramesh hear every line, not only the painful one, and the open question let him find the praise himself instead of being told to cheer up.

qa.q: What was the review like for Ramesh before Usha read it aloud?
qa.a: For Ramesh it felt like a telling-off about slow updates; the praise about the billing fix, the juniors and the clients did not register at all.

grounding: A team lead sees an employee leave a good review convinced it was criticism, reads the whole page aloud and asks what else it says.

passage:
Sunday, 11:40 pm

Stall day. The bit I keep replaying: the man who said my chai was lukewarm and made a face. Nitin shrugged it off. I've been chewing on it for five hours and was ready to tell Nitin we should drop the Sunday stall.
Before deciding anything, doing what I promised myself. Two columns.
Went well:
1. Sold out of poha by eleven.
2. The college group came back for the third week in a row.
3. Nitin and I didn't snap at each other once, even in the rush.
Didn't go well:
1. Chai went lukewarm in the flask around noon.
Looking at it written down: the lukewarm chai is real, and it needs fixing. But it's one flask, not the whole stall. Plan: buy a second flask and keep one on the stove. Not quitting.

Tanvir

qa.q: What sold out by eleven?
qa.a: The poha sold out by eleven.

qa.q: How was Tanvir feeling before making the two columns?
qa.a: Tanvir felt stung and discouraged by the complaint, replaying it for five hours and ready to give up the Sunday stall.

qa.q: What did the two-column list do well?
qa.a: It set three real successes next to the one problem, so Tanvir saw the chai issue at its true size and planned a fix instead of quitting, without pretending the complaint was wrong.

qa.q: How might Nitin see the decision to keep going?
qa.a: Nitin, who shrugged the complaint off, would likely feel relieved that the stall continues and glad the problem got a practical fix. 👍

grounding: An adult lists three things that went well beside the one that did not before deciding what to do, which corrects the bias without denying the criticism.

passage:
25 December

Went with Mumma to Elizabeth's family Christmas lunch. Elizabeth had pinned my pencil drawing of her grandmother's hands on the fridge, the one from last month. Her aunt stood in front of it for ages and said it looked like it could breathe.
I said, "It just came out okay by luck. Anyone could do it if they sat long enough." Elizabeth rolled her eyes and said I spent eleven evenings on it. That's not skill though, that's just being stubborn.
Then her cousin asked if I'd draw their dog, and I said no, because next time it won't work out and everyone will see I'm not actually good.
Plum cake was great 🎄 The drawing thing is sitting in my stomach like a stone.

Shreya

qa.q: What did Elizabeth's aunt say about the drawing?
qa.a: That it looked like it could breathe.

qa.q: Why does calling the drawing luck feel safer to Shreya?
qa.a: Shreya feels anxious about being exposed as "not actually good"; if the drawing was luck, the praise can't raise expectations, so there is nothing to fail at next time.

qa.q: What could Shreya try the next time someone praises a drawing?
qa.a: Shreya could just say "thank you, it took eleven evenings" and even try the dog drawing, treating the praise as information instead of a trap.

qa.q: How might Elizabeth feel hearing Shreya call it luck?
qa.a: Elizabeth seems exasperated, having watched Shreya spend eleven evenings on it and pinned it up proudly; the brush-off may feel as if Elizabeth's praise does not count either.

grounding: A teenager praised for a drawing calls it luck and something anyone could do, so the negative self-view stays untouched.

passage:
The results went up on the notice board of the Sangrur college the week before Lohri, and Avni's name sat at the top of the economics list. Deepika, who rode the same bus from the village, spotted it first and shook Avni's arm. "First! In the whole year!"
Avni shrugged, pulling her shawl tighter against the fog. "The paper was easy. Everyone must have got good marks."
"I got fifty-two," Deepika said.
"Then the checking was loose."
On the bus home, past carts stacked with sugarcane, Avni went quiet, then brought up the maths test in October where she had scored badly. "That one shows where I really stand."
Deepika stared. "So the bad one counts and the good one doesn't?"
Avni looked out of the window and didn't answer.

qa.q: Where did Avni's name appear?
qa.a: At the top of the economics list on the notice board of the Sangrur college.

qa.q: Why might Avni insist the paper was easy?
qa.a: Avni seems uneasy with the success; calling the paper easy keeps her old picture of herself safe, while the bad October maths test feels like the true measure.

qa.q: What question could help Avni judge her results more fairly?
qa.a: Avni could apply one rule to both results: if an easy paper explains the top mark, why did Deepika get fifty-two, and why should only the October test count?

qa.q: How might Deepika feel when Avni says the checking was loose?
qa.a: Deepika, who got fifty-two, may feel quietly belittled and baffled that a win Deepika was excited to see is dismissed so fast.

grounding: A student who topped a paper calls it an easy exam and a fluke, while an earlier bad test is treated as the real proof.
